claims.text: High-melting refractory materials can be modeled in the solid state using DFT-level atomic interactions.
Refractory materials have high melting temperatures.
The two-phase coexistence method initializes a simulation cell containing both solid and liquid phases.
Under constant-energy or constant-temperature conditions, the solid-liquid interface can evolve naturally toward phase equilibrium.
The two-phase coexistence method and the Z method are interchangeable descriptions of the proposed method.
Coexistence simulations should be performed at temperatures close to the melting point.
Sufficient simulation-cell size and simulation time are required to equilibrate the solid-liquid interface.
Refractory materials require high-temperature melting simulations.
The evolving solid-liquid interface mediates establishment of equilibrium between the solid and liquid phases.
Direct sampling of coexisting solid and liquid regions permits melting properties to be extracted from the equilibrium state.
Phase-boundary dynamics allow expensive thermodynamic integration to be bypassed.
The proposed method will yield the melting temperature.
The proposed method will yield the entropy and enthalpy of fusion.
The proposed method will yield the volume change at melting.
The proposed method will have accuracy comparable to full ab initio free-energy calculations.
The proposed method will reduce computational expense enough to support higher-throughput evaluations.
Conventional ab initio free-energy approaches use extensive thermodynamic integration based on ab initio molecular dynamics.
The reliability of the method depends on achieving and maintaining a well-resolved equilibrium solid-liquid interface.
Interface instability or dominant finite-size effects can prevent accurate reproduction of melting properties.
The magnitude of the computational-cost reduction and any deviations in predicted melting properties require direct benchmarking.
